findings.source_passage: Cannibals? who is not a cannibal? I tell you it will be more tolerable for the Fejee that salted down a lean missionary in his cellar against a coming famine
findings.source_locator: paragraph 5, 'Cannibals? who is not a cannibal?'
findings.why_it_matters: 'Cannibals? who is not a cannibal?' is one of the most famous, widely-quoted lines in Moby-Dick; the draft retains the question but strips 'I tell you' and the full rhetorical formulation 'salted down a lean missionary in his cellar against a coming famine,' collapsing the comic specificity that makes the line iconic.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'Cannibals? who is not a cannibal? I tell you it will be more tolerable for the Fejee that salted down a lean missionary in his cellar against a coming famine; it will be more tolerable for that provident Fejee, I say, in the day of judgment, than for thee…'

findings.source_passage: that a man should eat a newly murdered thing of the sea, and eat it too by its own light. But no doubt the first man that ever murdered an ox was regarded as a murderer; perhaps he was hung; and if he had been put on his trial by oxen, he certainly would have been
findings.source_locator: paragraph 5, 'It is not, perhaps, entirely because…'
findings.why_it_matters: The mock-juridical fantasy of the ox's trial ('if he had been put on his trial by oxen, he certainly would have been; and he certainly deserved it if any murderer does') is a voice-defining satirical digression; the draft reduces it to a single flat sentence ('the first butcher of an ox was surely deemed a murderer'), erasing the ironic register entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the trial-by-oxen conceit, including 'perhaps he was hung' and the deadpan 'he certainly deserved it if any murderer does'—even in compressed form the juridical joke must survive.

findings.source_passage: nailest geese to the ground and feastest on their bloated livers in thy paté-de-foie-gras
findings.why_it_matters: The archaic second-person ('nailest… feastest') and the grotesque image of nailing geese to the ground is the rhetorical peak of the paragraph's indictment; the draft replaces it with the bare noun 'gourmand of paté-de-foie-gras,' erasing the voice and the visceral cruelty charge.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'nailest geese to the ground and feastest on their bloated livers in thy paté-de-foie-gras' verbatim; the archaic syntax is essential to the satirical register.

findings.source_passage: The head looks a sort of reproachfully at him, with an 'Et tu Brute!' expression.
findings.why_it_matters: The 'Et tu Brute!' punchline is the comic payoff of the calves'-brains joke and an interpretively distinctive moment of Melville's ironic anthropomorphism; the draft drops the entire closing image.
findings.suggested_fix: Append the reproachful-head image and its 'Et tu Brute!' tag to the calves'-brain passage, even in one compressed sentence.

findings.source_passage: smelling something like old Amsterdam housewives' dough-nuts or oly-cooks, when fresh. They have such an eatable look that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off.
findings.why_it_matters: The oly-cooks simile and the 'most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off' are quintessential Ishmael voice—sensory, comic, culturally specific; the draft retains only 'crisp, brown scraps,' gutting the passage's humor and texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the dough-nut/oly-cooks smell and the 'self-denying stranger' sentence; these are not mere filler but voice-establishing comic detail.

findings.source_passage: Look at your knife-handle, there, my civilized and enlightened gourmand dining off that roast beef, what is that handle made of?—what but the bones of the brother of the very ox you are eating?
findings.why_it_matters: The direct-address harangue ('Look at your knife-handle, there, my civilized and enlightened gourmand') with its rhetorical question structure is the chapter's satirical climax; the draft converts it to a flat declarative ('look at thy knife-handle: bones of the brother of the ox thou eatest'), losing the performative indignation.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the interrogative address form and the doubled ironic epithet 'civilized and enlightened gourmand' to preserve the satirical voice.

summary: The draft commits three high-severity failures—mangling the famous 'who is not a cannibal' passage, stripping the trial-by-oxen satirical digression, and erasing 'nailest geese to the ground'—plus three medium voice-flattenings, together gutting the chapter's satirical register and its most quotable moments.
